title: NICE
description: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence — wisdom teeth extraction (TA1).

subjects.title: Wisdom teeth extraction
subjects.description: NICE Technology Appraisal 1 (March 2000): when impacted third molars should and should not be surgically removed.

workflows.title: Decision to extract an impacted third molar
workflows.overview:
## 1. Default position

Prophylactic removal of **pathology-free** impacted third molars **should be discontinued in the NHS**. The presence of an impaction, on its own, is not an indication for surgery.

## 2. Routine dental care still applies

For pathology-free impacted third molars, the standard programme of dental care by dental practitioners and paraprofessional staff need be **no different**. The patient stays on normal recall and is examined at usual check-ups; the tooth is monitored, not operated on.

## 3. Look for genuine pathology

Surgical removal is **limited to patients with evidence of pathology**. Document the indication and diagnosis in the notes (audit requirement).

### Indications for surgical removal (section 1.3)
- **Unrestorable caries**
- **Non-treatable pulpal and/or periapical pathology**
- **Cellulitis, abscess and osteomyelitis**
- **Internal or external resorption** of the tooth or adjacent teeth
- **Fracture of tooth**
- **Disease of the follicle** including cyst or tumour
- Tooth or teeth **impeding surgery or reconstructive jaw surgery**
- Tooth involved in or within the **field of tumour resection**

## 4. Plaque and pericoronitis: special attention

Plaque formation is a **risk factor** but is **not in itself an indication for surgery**.

### Pericoronitis branch
1. **First episode** of pericoronitis → **not** an indication for surgery, *unless particularly severe*
2. **Second or subsequent episodes** → considered the **appropriate indication** for surgery

The degree to which severity or recurrence rate should influence the decision remains unclear; document the episode count and severity at every visit.

## 5. Shared decision conversation before surgery

Where extraction is indicated, cover the risks of the procedure in plain language before consenting:

- **Temporary or permanent nerve damage**
- **Alveolar osteitis** (dry socket)
- **Infection**
- **Haemorrhage**
- **Temporary local swelling, pain and restricted mouth opening**
- **General anaesthesia risks** where GA is needed, including rare and unpredictable death

A patient with a pathology-free impacted third molar who undergoes surgery is being **exposed to the risk of a surgical procedure unnecessarily**.

## 6. Audit and review

- Record the **indication and diagnosis** for every wisdom-tooth extraction (per section 7.1)
- Review patients currently on a wisdom-tooth extraction waiting list against this guidance; case-note review or recall to a review clinic
- Use the patient information in section 10 of TA1 to inform any review-clinic letters

firstPrinciples.title: There is no reliable evidence that prophylactic removal of healthy impacted wisdom teeth benefits patients
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Removal of wisdom teeth is one of the most common surgical procedures in the UK. Whether the asymptomatic impacted third molar is a problem to fix or a tooth to monitor is the central question.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The evidence base, plainly stated

NICE TA1 settled this in one sentence: there is no reliable research evidence to support a health benefit to patients from the prophylactic removal of pathology-free impacted third molar teeth [1]. The default for an asymptomatic impacted wisdom tooth is therefore observation, not extraction.

## What this changes about routine care

A pathology-free impacted third molar does not pull the patient out of the standard recall pathway. The standard routine programme of dental care need be no different for these teeth [2]. The dentist examines the tooth at usual check-ups, monitors it, and intervenes only if pathology develops.

## What changed in the NHS

Before TA1, up to 44% of wisdom-tooth removals may have been inappropriate, and after the 1997 Royal College guidelines around 22% may still have been inappropriate [3]. TA1 made the discontinuation of prophylactic removal of pathology-free impacted third molars an explicit NHS recommendation [4].

citations.quote: There is no reliable research evidence to support a health benefit to patients from the prophylactic removal of pathology-free impacted third molar teeth.

The standard routine programme of dental care by dental practitioners and/or paraprofessional staff need be no different, in general, for pathology-free impacted third molars (those requiring no additional investigations or procedures).

Wide variations in the rates of this latter procedure across the country, which suggest that in the past, up to 44% of wisdom teeth removals and prophylactic surgery may have been inappropriate, have been reported. However, in recent years, changes in the practice of removal of wisdom teeth may have taken place in response to the Faculty of Dental Surgery of the Royal College of Surgeon's guidelines on the management of patients with third molar teeth (1997). Even so, some 22% of procedures may still be inappropriate.
The practice of prophylactic removal of pathology-free impacted third molars should be discontinued in the NHS.

firstPrinciples.title: Every third molar removal carries surgical risk, so a healthy impaction is exposure without benefit
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Surgical decisions are weighed by harm and benefit. When the benefit is zero, even small surgical harms tip the balance against intervention.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The standard risks of third molar surgery

NICE catalogues them: every procedure for the removal of an impacted third molar carries risk for the patient, including temporary or permanent nerve damage, alveolar osteitis, infection and haemorrhage, alongside temporary local swelling, pain and restricted mouth opening [1]. Where general anaesthesia is needed, additional risks apply, including rare and unpredictable death [2].

## Why this matters when there is no pathology

If there is no pathology, there is no health benefit being chased; the surgical risks are then carried for nothing. Such patients are being exposed to the risk of undertaking a surgical procedure unnecessarily [3].

## How this lands in the consent conversation

For patients with a genuine indication, the same risk list should be discussed openly: nerve damage, dry socket, infection, bleeding, swelling, trismus, and GA risks where applicable. The conversation is honest about why the surgery is worth those risks, and the alternative of monitoring is offered when the indication is borderline.

citations.quote: Every procedure for the removal of an impacted third molar carries risk for the patient, including temporary or permanent nerve damage, alveolar osteitis, infection and haemorrhage as well as temporary local swelling, pain and restricted mouth opening.
There are also risks associated with the need for general anaesthesia in some of these procedures, including rare and unpredictable death.
Such patients are therefore being exposed to the risk of undertaking a surgical procedure unnecessarily.

firstPrinciples.title: The pathologies that justify third molar surgery are a defined list
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: An indication for extraction is not a clinician's general impression of trouble; it is one of a specific set of pathologies set out by NICE. The list anchors the consent and the audit.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The list, in full

Surgical removal of impacted third molars should be limited to patients with evidence of pathology, including unrestorable caries, non-treatable pulpal and/or periapical pathology, cellulitis, abscess and osteomyelitis, internal or external resorption of the tooth or adjacent teeth, fracture of tooth, disease of follicle including cyst or tumour, tooth or teeth impeding surgery or reconstructive jaw surgery, and where a tooth is involved in or within the field of tumour resection [1].

## How the list is used

The list is the recorded indication for every extraction. Routinely record the indication for surgery and the diagnosis [2]. This is what makes individual practice auditable against TA1, and it is what differentiates a justifiable extraction from an inappropriate one.

## What is not on the list

A tooth is not extracted because it is impacted, because it has plaque on it, or because the patient finds it inconvenient. Plaque formation is a risk factor but is not in itself an indication for surgery [3].

citations.quote: Surgical removal of impacted third molars should be limited to patients with evidence of pathology. Such pathology includes unrestorable caries, non-treatable pulpal and/or periapical pathology, cellulitis, abscess and osteomyelitis, internal/external resorption of the tooth or adjacent teeth, fracture of tooth, disease of follicle including cyst/tumour, tooth/teeth impeding surgery or reconstructive jaw surgery, and when a tooth is involved in or within the field of tumour resection.

To enable dental practitioners to audit their own compliance with this guidance, it is recommended that all those who perform wisdom teeth extraction should routinely record the indication for surgery and the diagnosis (see section 1.3).
Plaque formation is a risk factor but is not in itself an indication for surgery.

firstPrinciples.title: A first episode of pericoronitis is not an indication for surgery; recurrence is
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Pericoronitis is the most common reason a partially erupted third molar comes to the dentist. The number of episodes, not the existence of one, drives the decision.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The evidence is uncertain, the rule is not

NICE accepts that the degree to which severity or recurrence rate of pericoronitis should influence the decision for surgical removal of a third molar remains unclear [1]. Even so, it commits to a clinical position: a first episode of pericoronitis, unless particularly severe, should not be considered an indication for surgery [2].

## When recurrence changes the answer

Second or subsequent episodes should be considered the appropriate indication for surgery [3]. This converts pericoronitis from an event into a pattern: one flare-up gets washed out, treated and reviewed; a second flare-up tips the tooth onto the extraction list.

## What this means at the chair

The practical move on a first episode is symptomatic management — local irrigation, oral hygiene reinforcement, occlusal adjustment of an over-erupting upper third molar where indicated, and antibiotics only when there are systemic signs. Document the episode in the notes so that the second presentation, when it comes, can be handled as a clear indication.

citations.quote: The degree to which the severity or recurrence rate of pericoronitis should influence the decision for surgical removal of a third molar remains unclear.
The evidence suggests that a first episode of pericoronitis, unless particularly severe, should not be considered an indication for surgery.
Second or subsequent episodes should be considered the appropriate indication for surgery.

firstPrinciples.title: Impaction is the consequence of inadequate space, obstruction or abnormal development
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Knowing why a wisdom tooth is impacted matters because the impaction itself is benign; the consequences that develop around it are what bring the patient back.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The mechanism

Third molars erupt last, usually between 18 and 24 years of age [1]. Impaction occurs when there is prevention of complete eruption due to lack of space, obstruction or development in an abnormal position [2]. The tooth may then erupt partially or not at all.

## Why impaction is monitored, not removed

Impaction by itself is not a disease; it is an anatomical state. It can be associated with pathological changes including pericoronitis, an increased risk of caries and periodontal disease in adjacent teeth, and orthodontic problems in later life [3]. Those associated changes, when they actually develop, are the lever for surgery, not the impaction itself.

## What this looks like in practice

A partially erupted lower third molar with a clean operculum, no caries, no resorption of the second molar, and no recurrent pericoronitis is monitored at routine recalls. The clinical eye is on the operculum, the distal of the second molar, the follicular outline on radiographs, and the pattern of any episodes of inflammation.

citations.quote: Permanent molar teeth normally erupt from the age of 6 onwards, with the third molars (wisdom teeth) being the last to erupt, usually between the ages of 18 and 24 years.
Impaction occurs when there is prevention of complete eruption due to lack of space, obstruction or development in an abnormal position. This may result in a tooth erupting partially or not at all.
Impaction may be associated with pathological changes including pericoronitis, an increased risk of caries and periodontal disease in adjacent teeth, and orthodontic problems in later life.
